text: Choosing the right chart type gets you most of the way there. The rest comes from color, layout and labels, which decide whether a reader gets your point in five seconds or gives up.

Before you color anything, ask what the color means. Categorical palettes separate groups with no order, like regions. Sequential palettes run light to dark for low-to-high values, like spend. Diverging palettes use two hues meeting at a neutral middle, for values above and below a meaningful center. Limit categorical colors to about five or six; beyond that, readers can't tell them apart.

About one in twelve men has some form of red-green color-vision deficiency, so never rely on red versus green alone. matplotlib ships a colorblind-friendly style you can switch on in a single line, and you should always add a second cue too, like a direct label or a different marker.

Five layout habits. Write the title as the finding, not the topic. Label values directly on the chart. Sort by value unless there's a natural order. Remove non-data ink like heavy borders and 3D effects. And start bars at zero.

The single most effective trick for an explanatory chart: make everything a quiet grey, and use one accent color for the thing you want the reader to notice. Here's the default version: four identical blue bars and a title that only names the topic.

Now the clarified version. Average spend by region: South two hundred eighty-three, North two hundred ninety-four, East two hundred ninety-six, West three hundred twenty-five. Sorted ascending, with West alone in orange-vermillion, a colorblind-safe accent, and a title that says exactly what to notice: West customers spend the most.

Use palettes for what they were designed for, never depend on red versus green alone, and let grey plus one accent color direct attention better than a full palette ever could. Next lesson: how charts mislead, sometimes on purpose, and how to keep yours honest.
